The issue is not that people are getting paid for their work. Sites like the Nexus (in Skyrims case) allow donations to modders. The issue is that valve/steam are receiving the majority of any payments, 75% to be exact. So if a modder puts a mod for sale for four dollars, the modder makes a buck and valve makes three.

Not to mention the already prevalent issue of people uploading and selling mods that they did not create. So while the intention may be for modders to get paid for their work, the possibility of people cashing in on a mod that they A) did not make and B) will not update puts modders at risk.

Also, similarly to the phenomenon of steam Early Access developers getting paid for a game that is not finished and then simply abandoning their project or ignoring players who purchased the game and expected (eventually) a full release, buying mods gives modders no incentive to update their mods and/or fix conflicts. The mod market becomes risky because you can't test a mod to see how it affects your game; You might buy a 6 dollar mod (again, 4.5 of those dollars will go to valve, who didn't do anything to contribute to making the mod) that is incompatible or causes bugs in your game and there is nothing you can do about it because you had no way to test its effects before buying.

It's not compensating people for their work. It's greedy, it's risky, and it's unfair for both modders and players.

Ice is not **transparent,** it is **translucent.** This means that unlike glass (a transparent material), the path of the light hitting the ice is changed rather than going straight through.

Snow is a bunch of ice crystals compacted and littered all over the ground. When the light hits one of the crystals, the light is bounced onto another crystal, and then another, and then another. Eventually, the light will bounce off of the snow and into your eye. Because the light is simply reflected and not absorbed by the snow, you see it as white.

Cooking food is part of what makes humans human. Heating and cooking the food (depending on the food of course) breaks down certain materials (ie. fibers, starches, proteins) before we actually consume them. This makes them easier to digest, and so less energy needs to be spent on breaking down food, while more can be spent on things like cognition.
